lines.text: **[PINNACLE CAPITAL PARTNERS, LLC]{.underline}**
**[ACCOUNT CONTROL AGREEMENT --- NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK]{.underline}**
**Prepared by Hargrave Stein & Collier LLP**
**787 Seventh Avenue, 40th Floor, New York, NY 10019**
**Hargrave Stein Matter No.: 2025-HSC-04417**
**PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT WORK PRODUCT**

*This playbook is prepared for the exclusive use of Pinnacle Capital Partners, LLC and its internal personnel in connection with the negotiation of deposit account control agreements across Pinnacle\'s secured lending portfolio. It is not intended for distribution to counterparties, depository banks, or borrower\'s counsel. This document reflects legal strategy and attorney mental impressions and is protected by the attorney-client privilege and work product doctrine.*
*Last Updated: April 2025*
*Lead Contact: Thomas Orr, Partner --- torr@hargravestein.com* *Associate Contact: Priya Nagarajan --- pnagarajan@hargravestein.com*
**[SECTION 1 --- INTRODUCTION AND PURPOSE]{.underline}**
**[1.1 --- Purpose of This Playbook]{.underline}**

This playbook serves as a standing reference for Hargrave Stein & Collier LLP attorneys and Pinnacle Capital Partners, LLC (\"Pinnacle\") internal personnel --- including Diana Whitford, Vice President -- Portfolio Management, and her team --- when negotiating deposit account control agreements (\"ACAs\" or \"DACAs\") with depository banks in connection with Pinnacle\'s revolving credit facilities and other secured lending transactions. The document is designed to be used as a real-time negotiation tool, enabling the assigned negotiator to respond promptly and consistently to bank markup positions without the delay inherent in seeking ad hoc client instructions on each individual issue.

The playbook is organized by issue category corresponding to common bank markup positions and covers the universe of substantive provisions typically found in tripartite ACAs among the secured party, the depositor (borrower or guarantor), and the depository bank. The issue categories addressed herein reflect the full range of provisions that have been the subject of negotiation in Pinnacle\'s ACA transactions over the past three years, including the firm\'s ongoing engagement with Ironbridge National Bank, N.A. in the Graycliff Industries, Inc. transaction (Matter No. 2025-HSC-04417).
For each issue category, the playbook sets forth three tiers of negotiating positions:

> **(a)** **Green --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred/Ideal Position.** This tier reflects the language contained in Pinnacle\'s form ACA, which represents Pinnacle\'s optimal position on each issue. The form ACA has been drafted to maximize Pinnacle\'s protections and to satisfy all requirements for \"control\" under UCC § 9-104. The preferred position should be the starting point in every negotiation and should be defended through at least the first round of counter-markups.

> **(b)** **Yellow --- Acceptable Fallback Positions.** This tier sets forth one or more compromise positions, with sample counter-language, that may be offered to the depository bank without further client approval from the deal team. These fallback positions have been pre-authorized by Diana Whitford and reflect the maximum concession that the deal team has determined is consistent with Pinnacle\'s risk parameters. Where multiple fallback positions are available within a single issue category, they are presented in order of preference (Fallback A is preferred over Fallback B, which is preferred over Fallback C), and the negotiator should exhaust each fallback before moving to the next.

> **(c)** **Red --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers.** This tier identifies positions that require express approval from the deal team (Diana Whitford or her designee) before any concession is offered. In certain cases, a bank position is identified as a \"hard stop\" --- meaning it cannot be accepted under any circumstances because it would destroy Pinnacle\'s control over the deposit accounts for UCC perfection purposes or otherwise create unacceptable legal risk. Hard-stop positions should be communicated clearly and firmly to bank counsel, with an explanation of the structural basis for the objection.

This playbook reflects Pinnacle\'s current risk posture as of April 2025 and should be revisited semi-annually or upon material changes in market practice, UCC amendments, or judicial decisions affecting deposit account control. The next scheduled review is October 2025. Any interim developments --- including significant judicial decisions, regulatory guidance, or changes in Pinnacle\'s collateral policy --- should be communicated promptly to Thomas Orr or Priya Nagarajan for incorporation into the playbook.
**[1.2 --- Legal Framework: UCC Perfection over Deposit Accounts]{.underline}**

An understanding of the Uniform Commercial Code\'s requirements for perfection of a security interest in deposit accounts is essential to the effective negotiation of every ACA provision. This section provides a summary of the applicable legal framework, which should inform the negotiator\'s analysis of every bank markup.

**Perfection by Control Only.** Under UCC Article 9, \"control\" is the sole method of perfection of a security interest in a deposit account as original collateral. UCC § 9-312(b)(1) expressly provides that a security interest in a deposit account may be perfected only by control under UCC § 9-104. Filing a UCC-1 financing statement is insufficient to perfect a security interest in a deposit account as original collateral; although a financing statement may be filed to provide notice to third parties, it does not constitute perfection and does not establish priority. This distinguishes deposit accounts from most other categories of personal property collateral, where filing is the primary method of perfection. The consequence is that the ACA is not merely a supplemental perfection device --- it is the *only* mechanism by which Pinnacle can obtain a perfected security interest in its borrowers\' deposit account balances.
**Methods of Obtaining Control.** A secured party obtains \"control\" of a deposit account under UCC § 9-104 by one of three methods:

> **(i)** *Customer Method (§ 9-104(a)(1)):* The secured party becomes the bank\'s customer on the account --- i.e., the account is maintained in the secured party\'s name or the secured party is added as an account holder. This method is rarely used in commercial lending transactions because it requires the borrower to surrender account ownership.

> **(ii)** *Tripartite Agreement Method (§ 9-104(a)(2)):* The bank has agreed, in an authenticated record, to comply with instructions originated by the secured party directing the disposition of funds in the deposit account without further consent of the depositor. This is the method addressed by the standard ACA and is the method on which Pinnacle relies in substantially all of its secured lending transactions.

> **(iii)** *Bank-as-Secured-Party Method (§ 9-104(a)(3)):* The secured party is the depository bank itself. This method is available only to the bank at which the deposit account is maintained and is not relevant to Pinnacle\'s position as an external secured party.

**Pinnacle\'s ACA --- Tripartite Agreement Method.** Pinnacle\'s standard form ACA is designed to satisfy method (ii) --- the tripartite agreement among Pinnacle (as secured party), the borrower or guarantor (as depositor), and the depository bank. Under this method, the bank must agree in an authenticated record to comply with instructions originated by Pinnacle directing the disposition of the funds in the controlled accounts, and it must agree to do so *without further consent of the depositor*. This last requirement --- the absence of a depositor consent condition --- is the sine qua non of control under UCC § 9-104(a)(2). Every provision of the ACA must be evaluated through the lens of whether it preserves or undermines Pinnacle\'s \"control\" for purposes of this statutory requirement.

**Critical Caution --- Depositor Consent Conditions.** Any bank markup that conditions the bank\'s obligation to comply with Pinnacle\'s instructions on depositor consent, depositor notice, or any approval right of the depositor after delivery of a Notice of Exclusive Control (\"NOEC\") risks destroying the very control that the ACA is designed to establish and thus imperils perfection. The statutory language of UCC § 9-104(a)(2) is clear: the bank must agree to comply with the secured party\'s instructions \"without further consent of the debtor.\" A provision that reintroduces a depositor consent requirement --- whether framed as a \"consent,\" \"confirmation,\" \"acknowledgment,\" \"non-objection,\" or any equivalent formulation --- is fundamentally inconsistent with the statute and must be rejected. This principle is the single most important guideline in this playbook and applies across all issue categories.

**Cross-Reference to Article 8.** For the related but distinct question of whether the controlled account should be characterized as a \"securities account\" or \"deposit account\" --- and the implications of that characterization for the applicable control analysis --- see Section 2 of this playbook, which addresses UCC Article 8 vs. Article 9 control language.
**[1.3 --- Typical Transaction Context]{.underline}**

Pinnacle\'s ACAs most commonly arise in connection with revolving credit facilities where the applicable Credit Agreement requires delivery of ACAs over the borrower\'s principal deposit accounts within a specified post-closing period. The typical Credit Agreement provision is found in the post-closing obligations section (e.g., Credit Agreement § 6.14(b), or the equivalent provision in Pinnacle\'s form credit agreement), which requires delivery of fully executed ACAs within 30 to 60 calendar days of the closing date. In some transactions, the ACA delivery obligation is a condition to initial or subsequent advances; in others, it is a standalone covenant the breach of which constitutes an Event of Default if not cured within the applicable cure period.

Negotiators must track the applicable perfection deadline for each transaction and manage the bank negotiation timeline accordingly. Delays in ACA execution leave Pinnacle with an unperfected security interest in deposit account balances, creating a gap in the collateral package that exposes Pinnacle to the risk that a competing creditor --- including a bankruptcy trustee --- could obtain priority over the deposit account balances. In a bankruptcy scenario, an unperfected security interest in a deposit account is avoidable by the trustee under Section 544(a) of the Bankruptcy Code (the \"strong arm\" clause), with the result that the deposit account balances would be treated as unencumbered property of the estate. The urgency of timely ACA execution cannot be overstated.

In Pinnacle\'s current active matters, controlled deposit balances range from approximately \$10 million to \$50 million per borrower across multiple accounts. ACA negotiation effort should be proportionate to the value of the collateral at stake. For transactions involving controlled deposit balances in excess of \$25 million, the full negotiation playbook should be applied with rigor; for smaller balances, the negotiator retains discretion to prioritize critical structural issues (Sections 2 through 5) and accept reasonable bank positions on secondary issues (Sections 6 through 13) to expedite execution.
**[1.4 --- How to Use This Playbook]{.underline}**

The playbook is organized around the three-tier framework described in Section 1.1 above: **Green** (preferred position), **Yellow** (acceptable fallback --- pre-authorized for concession without further client approval), and **Red** (escalation required before any concession is offered). This framework applies to each issue category covered in Sections 2 through 14.
When a bank returns a markup of the ACA, the negotiator should follow the process set forth below:

> **Step 1 --- Issue Mapping.** Map each substantive bank change to the corresponding playbook section. If a bank change does not correspond to a specific playbook section, flag it for review by Thomas Orr or Priya Nagarajan.
> **Step 2 --- Tier Classification.** For each bank change, determine whether the bank\'s position falls within the Green, Yellow, or Red tier for the applicable issue category.

> **Step 3 --- Counter-Markup Preparation.** Prepare a redline response that (a) rejects all Red-tier bank positions and restores Pinnacle\'s preferred language (unless escalation has resulted in client authorization to concede), (b) addresses Yellow-tier issues by first attempting to achieve the Green position and offering fallback language only if the bank has rejected or pushed back on the preferred position, and (c) accepts any bank changes that are consistent with Pinnacle\'s preferred position or are immaterial.

A critical reminder: even where a fallback position is pre-authorized under this playbook, the negotiator should attempt to achieve the preferred (Green) position in the first counter-markup. Fallback language should be offered only after the bank has rejected or pushed back on the preferred position in a prior round of negotiation. Opening with a fallback position signals unnecessary flexibility and may invite further bank pushback on other issues.

The playbook is designed to be used in conjunction with Pinnacle\'s form ACA, which should be delivered to the depository bank as the initial draft in every transaction where Pinnacle controls the documentation process. Where the bank insists on using its own form ACA, the negotiator should map the bank\'s form against Pinnacle\'s form, identify all deviations, and treat each deviation as a bank markup subject to the playbook\'s three-tier analysis.
**[SECTION 2 --- UCC ARTICLE 8 vs. ARTICLE 9 CONTROL LANGUAGE]{.underline}**
**[2.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**

Pinnacle\'s form ACA uses \"entitlement order\" language drawn from UCC Article 8 (specifically, UCC § 8-102(a)(8)) rather than the Article 9 \"instruction\" terminology found in UCC § 9-104(a)(2). This is a deliberate drafting choice that reflects Pinnacle\'s belt-and-suspenders approach to perfection of its security interest in controlled deposit accounts.

The rationale for using Article 8 language is as follows: if the deposit account can be characterized or re-characterized as a \"securities account\" within the meaning of UCC § 8-501 --- for example, because the account is a money market deposit account, a sweep account that invests in securities or money market instruments, or an account that holds financial assets credited to the depositor\'s account --- then control under Article 8 (via the securities intermediary\'s agreement to comply with \"entitlement orders\" as defined in UCC § 8-102(a)(8)) provides an additional layer of perfection beyond Article 9 control. Under UCC § 8-106(d), a purchaser (including a secured party) has \"control\" of a security entitlement if the securities intermediary has agreed to comply with entitlement orders originated by the purchaser without further consent of the entitlement holder. By incorporating this concept into the ACA, Pinnacle obtains dual-track perfection: control under Article 9 (as to the deposit account) and control under Article 8 (as to any security entitlement).

\"Entitlement order\" is defined under UCC § 8-102(a)(8) as a notification communicated to a securities intermediary directing transfer or redemption of a financial asset to which a specified person has acquired a security entitlement. Pinnacle\'s form ACA incorporates this term in Section 2(a) of the ACA, which provides that the bank agrees to comply with \"entitlement orders\" originated by the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts, thereby satisfying the control requirements of both UCC § 8-106 and UCC § 9-104. The operative provision of the form ACA reads, in relevant part:

> *\"The Bank agrees that it will comply with entitlement orders originated by the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts without further consent of the Depositor. For purposes of this Agreement, \'entitlement order\' has the meaning assigned to such term in Section 8-102(a)(8) of the UCC. The Bank further agrees that it will comply with instructions originated by the Secured Party directing disposition of the funds in the Accounts without further consent of the Depositor.\"*

This dual-track approach --- referencing both \"entitlement orders\" under Article 8 and \"instructions\" under Article 9 --- has been accepted by major depository banks in approximately 70% of Pinnacle\'s recent transactions without substantive objection. The remaining 30% of transactions have resulted in bank pushback, typically from bank counsel that maintains standardized ACA forms and resists deviations from their templates.
**[2.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**

The typical bank markup in this area involves the substitution of \"instruction\" (Article 9 terminology) for \"entitlement order\" (Article 8 terminology) in the operative control section of the ACA. The bank\'s position is generally that the controlled accounts are ordinary demand deposit accounts and not securities accounts, and that Article 8 terminology is therefore inapplicable and potentially misleading.

The bank\'s rationale is grounded in the following concerns: depository banks --- particularly those with standardized form ACAs reviewed by their own outside counsel --- resist Article 8 language because they do not wish to be treated as \"securities intermediaries\" within the meaning of UCC § 8-102(a)(14). Under Article 8, a securities intermediary is subject to a series of statutory duties, including the duty to comply with entitlement orders under UCC § 8-507, the duty to maintain a sufficient quantity of financial assets under UCC § 8-504, and the duty to exercise rights as directed by the entitlement holder under UCC § 8-506. Banks that are not in the business of maintaining securities accounts --- i.e., commercial banks as distinguished from broker-dealers and custodians --- are understandably reluctant to assume these additional obligations, which could alter the priority scheme applicable to the accounts and impose regulatory and operational burdens that the bank did not contemplate when establishing the deposit relationship.

Bank counsel (e.g., firms such as Blackmere Fox LLP, which has represented Ironbridge National Bank, N.A. in recent transactions) may cite OCC guidance or bank regulatory concerns as a basis for resisting securities-intermediary characterization. Some bank counsel have taken the position that characterizing an ordinary demand deposit account as a \"securities account\" could trigger regulatory reporting obligations or capital adequacy implications, although this argument is generally overstated and can be addressed by clarifying that the Article 8 language operates only as a conditional fall-back --- i.e., it applies only *if* the account is deemed to be a securities account, and does not independently re-characterize the account.
**[2.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**
Two pre-authorized fallback positions are available for this issue category, presented in order of preference:

**Fallback A --- Dual-Track Compromise.** Accept the bank\'s substitution of \"instruction\" for \"entitlement order\" in the operative control section (Section 2(a) of the ACA), but add a standalone representation and covenant by the bank providing that if any Account is at any time deemed a \"securities account\" under UCC Article 8, the bank agrees to comply with entitlement orders originated by the Secured Party without further consent of the Depositor. This approach preserves the belt-and-suspenders protection while accommodating the bank\'s concern about day-one Article 8 characterization. The following sample language should be inserted as a new subsection:

> *\"Notwithstanding the foregoing, if any Account is at any time deemed to be a \'securities account\' (as defined in Section 8-501 of the UCC), the Bank agrees to treat the Secured Party as the \'entitlement holder\' (as defined in Section 8-102(a)(7) of the UCC) with respect to such Account and to comply with \'entitlement orders\' (as defined in Section 8-102(a)(8) of the UCC) originated by the Secured Party with respect to such Account without further consent of the Depositor.\"*

This language has been well received by bank counsel in prior transactions because it is explicitly conditional (\"if any Account is at any time deemed to be a \'securities account\'\") and does not, on its face, characterize the accounts as securities accounts or the bank as a securities intermediary. It addresses the bank\'s core concern while preserving Pinnacle\'s fallback Article 8 protection.

**Fallback B --- Article 9 Only with Protective Representation.** If the bank rejects Fallback A, accept Article 9-only \"instruction\" language throughout the operative control provisions, but require the bank to add a representation and covenant confirming that it has not entered into, and will not enter into, any agreement with any other party pursuant to which it agrees to comply with instructions or entitlement orders concerning any Account. This representation ensures that even without Article 8 belt-and-suspenders language, Pinnacle\'s Article 9 control is unimpaired by competing agreements that could affect priority under UCC § 9-327. The relevant sample language for this representation is set forth in Section 12 of this playbook (Representations and Warranties).

Fallback B is a meaningful concession and should be offered only if Fallback A has been expressly rejected by the bank. When offering Fallback B, the negotiator should present it as the final position on this issue and make clear that Pinnacle is not prepared to accept Article 9-only language without some form of protective representation regarding competing agreements.
**[2.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
The following scenarios require escalation or represent hard-stop positions:

> • If the bank refuses both Fallback A and Fallback B and insists on \"instruction\"-only language without any protective representation regarding competing agreements, **escalate to Diana Whitford**. While Article 9-only language, standing alone, is sufficient for perfection, the absence of any representation regarding competing agreements creates a risk that the bank may have entered into (or may in the future enter into) a competing control agreement with another secured party, which could affect Pinnacle\'s priority under UCC § 9-327.

> • If the bank takes the position that the ACA does not confer \"control\" within the meaning of UCC § 9-104(a)(2) --- i.e., if the bank\'s markup conditions compliance with Pinnacle\'s instructions on depositor consent even after delivery of a NOEC --- this is a **hard stop**. Such language destroys perfection and cannot be accepted under any circumstances. The negotiator should escalate immediately to Thomas Orr and Diana Whitford and should consider engaging a replacement bank if the depository bank is unwilling to cure the deficiency.

**Guiding Principle:** Preserving valid \"control\" under UCC § 9-104 is non-negotiable. Any provision that makes the bank\'s compliance with Secured Party instructions contingent on Depositor approval post-NOEC delivery vitiates the control necessary for perfection and must be rejected outright, regardless of any other concessions the bank may offer on other issues.
**[SECTION 3 --- EXCLUSIVE vs. SPRINGING CONTROL MECHANICS]{.underline}**
**[3.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
Pinnacle\'s form ACA uses a \"springing exclusive control\" model. Under this model, the control mechanic operates in two phases:

> **Phase 1 --- Pre-NOEC (Ordinary Course Operations).** Prior to the delivery of a NOEC by Pinnacle to the bank, the Depositor (e.g., Graycliff Industries, Inc.) is permitted to operate the controlled accounts in the ordinary course of business --- originating debits, credits, wire transfers, ACH transactions, and other transfers --- without Pinnacle\'s prior consent. During this phase, Pinnacle\'s control exists as a legal matter (because the bank has agreed to comply with Pinnacle\'s instructions without the Depositor\'s consent), but Pinnacle does not exercise that control on a day-to-day basis. The Depositor retains operational access to the accounts and uses them for working capital management, vendor payments, payroll, and other business purposes.

> **Phase 2 --- Post-NOEC (Exclusive Control).** Upon delivery of a NOEC by Pinnacle to the bank, exclusive control springs to Pinnacle, and the bank must cease complying with the Depositor\'s instructions and instead comply solely with Pinnacle\'s instructions regarding the disposition of funds in the controlled accounts. The Depositor\'s operational access is extinguished, and the bank must freeze the accounts (or redirect funds as directed by Pinnacle) until the ACA is terminated or the NOEC is rescinded.

The springing control model is preferred over day-one exclusive control for several reasons. First, it permits the borrower to operate its business without the operational burden of seeking Pinnacle\'s approval for each transaction in the controlled accounts, which would be commercially impracticable in a performing credit relationship. Second, it preserves Pinnacle\'s ability to lock down the accounts upon a triggering event --- typically the occurrence of an Event of Default under the Credit Agreement --- thereby protecting the collateral at the moment when protection is most needed. Third, the springing model is the market-standard approach in leveraged lending and middle-market credit transactions and is generally accepted by depository banks without fundamental objection.

The critical element of the springing control model --- and the element most frequently targeted by bank markups --- is the bank\'s unconditional agreement to comply with Pinnacle\'s instructions after NOEC delivery **without any requirement to obtain the Depositor\'s consent, verify the occurrence of an Event of Default, or otherwise qualify its compliance obligation.** The form ACA achieves this by providing:

> *\"Upon the Bank\'s receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control delivered by the Secured Party in accordance with Section \[●\], the Bank shall comply exclusively with instructions of the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts and shall not comply with instructions of the Depositor with respect to the Accounts. The Bank shall not require the consent, approval, or authorization of the Depositor as a condition to its compliance with the Secured Party\'s instructions following receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control.\"*
**[3.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
Banks frequently push back on the springing control mechanic in two principal ways:

**Processing and Wind-Down Carve-Outs.** Banks commonly insert a carve-out allowing the Depositor to continue operating the accounts even after delivery of a NOEC unless and until the bank has had time to process and implement the NOEC through its internal systems. The bank\'s concern is operational: upon receipt of a NOEC, the bank must update its systems to redirect account access, disable the Depositor\'s online banking credentials, freeze automated payment templates, and coordinate across multiple internal departments (operations, compliance, legal, and relationship management). Some banks seek to retain the right to honor previously issued or pending Depositor instructions --- such as outstanding checks, ACH batches in process, wire transfers that have been initiated but not yet completed, and standing payment orders --- for a specified period after NOEC delivery.

**Certification of Default.** Some banks seek to add a requirement that the NOEC include a certification that an Event of Default has occurred under the Credit Agreement, or that the NOEC specify the nature of the triggering event. The bank\'s rationale is that it does not want to be placed in the position of freezing its customer\'s accounts based on an unsubstantiated instruction from the Secured Party, and that a certification provides the bank with a degree of assurance (and potential legal cover) that the NOEC has been properly issued.

Both of these pushback positions raise concerns, but they are not equally problematic. The processing carve-out is an operational issue that can be addressed through a limited wind-down period (see Fallback A below). The certification requirement, however, is a structural issue that must be firmly resisted, as discussed in Fallback B and the Red-tier triggers below.
**[3.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**

**Fallback A --- Operational Wind-Down Period.** Accept a limited wind-down period --- not exceeding one (1) business day after the bank\'s receipt and confirmation of the NOEC --- during which the bank may honor Depositor instructions that were originated by and accepted by the bank prior to the bank\'s receipt of the NOEC. After the expiration of the wind-down period, the bank must comply exclusively with Pinnacle\'s instructions. This fallback acknowledges the operational reality that the bank cannot instantaneously freeze all account activity and allows a brief period for in-process transactions to settle. The following sample language may be offered:

> *\"The Bank shall comply with the Secured Party\'s instructions with respect to the Accounts commencing on the business day immediately following the Bank\'s receipt and confirmation of a Notice of Exclusive Control, provided that the Bank may honor instructions of the Depositor that were originated by and accepted by the Bank prior to the Bank\'s receipt of such Notice, but only to the extent such instructions have not been completed as of such time.\"*

Key drafting points for this fallback language: (i) the wind-down applies only to Depositor instructions that were *originated and accepted* before the NOEC was received --- the bank may not accept new Depositor instructions after NOEC receipt; (ii) the wind-down is limited to one business day; and (iii) after the wind-down, the bank\'s compliance with Pinnacle\'s instructions is exclusive and unconditional.

**Fallback B --- No Certification of Default.** The NOEC shall not be required to certify or specify the nature of the Event of Default or other triggering event; a statement by Pinnacle that it is exercising its rights under the ACA shall be sufficient. This position is non-negotiable even as a fallback --- it is a structural requirement, not a concession. The bank is not a party to the Credit Agreement and is not in a position to evaluate the occurrence or continuation of an Event of Default; imposing a certification requirement effectively delegates to the bank a contractual interpretation function that belongs exclusively to the Secured Party. Moreover, a certification requirement creates the risk that the bank will refuse to comply with a NOEC on the ground that the certification is incomplete or inaccurate, thereby undermining Pinnacle\'s ability to exercise control at the moment when it is most critical. The NOEC form attached to the ACA should contain a simple statement:

> *\"The Secured Party hereby notifies the Bank that the Secured Party is exercising its rights under Section \[●\] of the Account Control Agreement dated as of \[●\], and directs the Bank to comply exclusively with instructions of the Secured Party with respect to the Accounts.\"*
No additional certification, explanation, or supporting documentation should be required.
**[3.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**
The following positions represent escalation triggers or hard stops:

> • Any bank markup requiring the Depositor\'s consent to the NOEC, or requiring the bank to verify the occurrence of an Event of Default before complying with Pinnacle\'s post-NOEC instructions, is a **hard stop**. Such a provision is fundamentally inconsistent with UCC § 9-104(a)(2) control and vitiates perfection. Reject outright and escalate to Thomas Orr and Diana Whitford.

> • Any wind-down period exceeding two (2) business days --- **escalate to Diana Whitford**. While a one-business-day wind-down is the pre-authorized fallback, a two-business-day period may be acceptable in certain circumstances depending on the bank\'s operational constraints and the size of the controlled balances. Wind-down periods of three or more business days are presumptively unacceptable and require express deal-team approval.

> • Any carve-out permitting the bank to continue honoring *new* Depositor instructions (as opposed to previously originated instructions in process) after NOEC delivery --- **hard stop**. This is functionally equivalent to requiring the Depositor\'s consent and destroys the springing-control mechanic entirely.
**[SECTION 4 --- NOEC COMPLIANCE PERIOD]{.underline}**
**[4.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**

Pinnacle\'s form ACA requires the bank to begin complying with Pinnacle\'s exclusive instructions within two (2) business days of the bank\'s receipt of a NOEC. This two-business-day period represents the time allowed for the bank to process the NOEC through its internal systems --- including updating account access controls, freezing automated payment instructions, and coordinating across the bank\'s operations, compliance, and legal departments --- and to transition operational control of the accounts from the Depositor to the Secured Party.

The rationale for a two-business-day period is straightforward: speed of lock-down is essential in distressed situations. When Pinnacle delivers a NOEC, it is typically because the borrower has experienced an Event of Default --- which may include a payment default, a financial covenant breach, a material adverse change, or a triggering event under the Credit Agreement\'s acceleration provisions. In such circumstances, the borrower may be actively dissipating assets or diverting cash from the controlled accounts. Every additional business day between the NOEC and the bank\'s compliance with Pinnacle\'s exclusive instructions is a day during which the borrower can withdraw, transfer, or encumber the controlled deposit balances. A two-business-day compliance period balances the bank\'s legitimate operational needs against Pinnacle\'s need for prompt access to its collateral.
**[4.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**
Banks commonly request a longer compliance period, typically five (5) business days, and sometimes as long as seven to ten (10) business days. The bank\'s cited justifications typically include:
> • Internal processing requirements, including the need to update account authorization profiles in the bank\'s core banking system;
> • Coordination across multiple bank departments --- operations, compliance, legal, and relationship management --- each of which may need to review and approve the transition of account control;

> • The complexity of freezing automated payment instructions, including ACH origination agreements, wire transfer templates, standing payment orders, and sweep account configurations, which may require manual intervention; and

> • Regulatory and compliance review, including potential Bank Secrecy Act / Anti-Money Laundering considerations if the NOEC results in changes to the account\'s beneficial ownership or authorized signers.

In the current Ironbridge matter (Hargrave Stein internal reference 2025-HSC-04417), Ironbridge National Bank, N.A. has proposed a five (5) business-day compliance period in its Turn 1 markup of the ACA. Blackmere Fox LLP, bank counsel, has cited the bank\'s internal processing protocol and the involvement of multiple departments as the basis for the extended period.
**[4.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**

**Authorized Fallback --- Three (3) Business Days Maximum.** Pinnacle\'s deal team has pre-authorized a maximum NOEC compliance period of three (3) business days. This represents the outer boundary of acceptability without further client approval and reflects the deal team\'s assessment that a three-business-day period provides adequate time for the bank\'s operational transition while limiting Pinnacle\'s exposure to dissipation risk during the compliance window.
The following sample counter-language should be used:

> *\"The Bank shall comply with the Secured Party\'s instructions with respect to the Accounts beginning no later than the third (3rd) Business Day following the Bank\'s receipt and authentication of a Notice of Exclusive Control delivered in accordance with Section \[●\].\"*

**Negotiation Tactic.** Open with the preferred two-business-day position in the first counter-markup. If the bank rejects the two-business-day period (which is likely, given that Ironbridge has proposed five business days), offer three business days in the second counter-markup as a \"significant concession\" to close the issue. Frame the concession as movement toward the bank\'s position (from two days to three days, representing a 50% increase in the compliance window) and emphasize that this represents Pinnacle\'s final position. Avoid moving directly from two days to five days, as doing so forfeits negotiating leverage on this issue and signals willingness to accept the bank\'s initial position.
**[4.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**

> • Any NOEC compliance period exceeding three (3) business days requires express approval from Diana Whitford before the negotiator may agree. The negotiator should present the escalation with the following information: (a) the bank\'s stated rationale for the longer period, (b) the total controlled deposit balances at stake, and (c) an assessment of the dissipation risk during the extended compliance window.

> • If the bank insists on five (5) or more business days, escalate and assess whether the delay risk is proportionate to the controlled deposit balances at stake. In a matter where total controlled deposits are in the range of \$38 million --- as in the current Graycliff Industries/Ironbridge National Bank transaction, where the three controlled accounts (●●●●-4471, ●●●●-4472, and ●●●●-4473) hold approximately \$38,150,000 in aggregate --- a five-business-day delay could expose Pinnacle to material dissipation risk, particularly if the borrower is aware that a NOEC has been delivered and is motivated to divert funds before the lock-down takes effect.
**[SECTION 5 --- CONFLICTING INSTRUCTIONS AND PRIORITY WATERFALL]{.underline}**
**[5.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**

Pinnacle\'s form ACA provides that in the event of conflicting instructions from the Secured Party and the Depositor regarding the disposition of funds in the controlled accounts, the Secured Party\'s instructions shall prevail in all circumstances, both before and after delivery of a NOEC.
This priority waterfall operates in two distinct contexts:

> **Pre-NOEC Context.** Prior to NOEC delivery, the Secured Party priority operates as a latent backstop. Because Pinnacle does not ordinarily issue instructions prior to a triggering event, conflicts between Pinnacle\'s instructions and the Depositor\'s instructions are unlikely in practice during the ordinary-course period. However, if they arise --- for example, because Pinnacle has delivered a standing instruction restricting certain types of transfers, or because Pinnacle has issued an instruction in connection with a cash management dispute that does not rise to the level of an Event of Default --- Pinnacle\'s instructions control, and the bank must follow them.

> **Post-NOEC Context.** After delivery of a NOEC, the Depositor\'s instruction rights are fully extinguished; the bank must comply exclusively with the Secured Party\'s instructions. In this context, the conflict scenario does not arise as a practical matter because the Depositor has no instruction rights to exercise. However, the form language is drafted broadly to ensure that any residual or unauthorized Depositor instruction is subordinated to the Secured Party\'s instruction.
The form language addressing conflicting instructions is as follows:
> *\"In the event of a conflict between instructions received from the Secured Party and instructions received from the Depositor, the Bank shall follow the instructions of the Secured Party.\"*

This language is intentionally broad and unconditional. It does not distinguish between the pre-NOEC and post-NOEC periods, does not require the Bank to inquire into the basis for the conflict, and does not give the Bank discretion to determine which instruction to follow. The simplicity of the provision is a feature, not a limitation --- it eliminates ambiguity and ensures that the Bank has a clear, unqualified contractual directive.
**[5.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**

Banks frequently resist unconditional Secured Party priority in the conflicting-instructions waterfall, particularly prior to NOEC delivery. The bank\'s concern is primarily operational and relates to its relationship with the Depositor as its customer. The bank\'s typical arguments include:

> • The Depositor is the bank\'s customer and the account holder; prior to NOEC delivery, the Depositor\'s instructions should control in the ordinary course because the Depositor is the party that established the banking relationship and that the bank owes its primary duties to.

> • The bank does not want to be caught between competing instructions from two parties, both of whom are the bank\'s contractual counterparties, without a clear contractual framework that protects the bank from liability for following one party\'s instructions over the other\'s.

> • Unconditional Secured Party priority prior to NOEC delivery could disrupt the Depositor\'s ordinary-course business operations and potentially trigger claims by the Depositor against the bank for failure to honor the Depositor\'s payment instructions.

A common bank markup is to provide that prior to NOEC delivery, the Depositor\'s instructions control (because the Depositor is the account holder and the bank\'s customer), and that Secured Party instructions take priority only after NOEC delivery. Some banks further condition post-NOEC priority on the bank\'s completion of its internal NOEC processing period (see Section 4 above), which effectively creates a gap period during which neither the Secured Party\'s nor the Depositor\'s instructions have clear contractual priority.
**[5.3 --- Acceptable Fallback Positions (Yellow)]{.underline}**

**Fallback A --- Bifurcated Priority (Pre- and Post-NOEC).** Accept a bifurcated structure that distinguishes between the pre-NOEC and post-NOEC periods. Under this structure: (i) prior to NOEC delivery, the Depositor\'s instructions control in the ordinary course, but the bank agrees to promptly notify Pinnacle of any instruction from the Depositor that conflicts with a standing instruction previously delivered by Pinnacle; and (ii) upon and after NOEC delivery, Pinnacle\'s instructions control exclusively and without qualification. The following sample language may be offered:

> *\"Prior to the Bank\'s receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control, the Bank shall follow the instructions of the Depositor with respect to the Accounts; provided that if the Bank receives an instruction from the Depositor that conflicts with a standing instruction previously delivered to the Bank by the Secured Party, the Bank shall promptly notify the Secured Party of such conflict and shall follow the Secured Party\'s standing instruction. Upon and after the Bank\'s receipt of a Notice of Exclusive Control, the Bank shall follow exclusively the instructions of the Secured Party and shall not be required to follow any instructions of the Depositor.\"*

This bifurcated structure is a reasonable compromise that addresses the bank\'s concern about pre-NOEC operational disruption while preserving Pinnacle\'s exclusive post-NOEC control. The notification obligation in the pre-NOEC period provides Pinnacle with visibility into potential conflicts and allows Pinnacle to take action (including issuing a NOEC if warranted) before the conflict results in dissipation of collateral.

**Fallback B --- Minimum Protective Language.** If Fallback A is rejected by the bank --- which is unusual, as the bifurcated structure is generally accepted by bank counsel --- accept a pre-NOEC regime in which Depositor instructions control without a standing-instruction override, but require the bank to agree that it will not permit any withdrawal, transfer, or disposition of funds from any Account in an amount exceeding a specified threshold without providing Pinnacle at least two (2) business days\' prior written notice. The threshold should be specified on a per-transaction basis and should be calibrated to the total controlled deposit balances; as a general guideline, the threshold should be set at the greater of \$500,000 or 5% of the aggregate account balances as of the date of the ACA. This fallback does not give Pinnacle instruction priority in the pre-NOEC period, but it provides an early-warning mechanism that enables Pinnacle to monitor large withdrawals and to deliver a NOEC if the withdrawal activity suggests dissipation.
**[5.4 --- Walk-Away / Escalation Triggers (Red)]{.underline}**

> • Any bank markup that conditions post-NOEC compliance with Pinnacle\'s instructions on Depositor consent, Depositor notice, or any third-party approval --- **hard stop**. This undermines UCC § 9-104 control and is not negotiable. The post-NOEC period is the critical juncture at which Pinnacle\'s control must be absolute, and any qualification of that control defeats the purpose of the ACA.

> • Any bank markup that gives the bank discretion to determine which conflicting instruction to follow --- rather than a contractually mandated waterfall --- **hard stop**. A discretionary standard (e.g., \"the Bank may, in its sole discretion, determine which instruction to follow\") is unacceptable because it introduces uncertainty into the priority scheme and leaves Pinnacle\'s collateral protection subject to the bank\'s judgment call at the moment of conflict.

> • Any markup that requires Pinnacle to indemnify the bank for following Pinnacle\'s instructions in a conflicting-instructions scenario --- **escalate to Diana Whitford**. This is likely acceptable if limited to post-NOEC instructions and subject to the indemnification parameters described in Section 8 of this playbook (including the carve-out for the bank\'s gross negligence, willful misconduct, or bad faith). However, an open-ended indemnification that covers the bank\'s losses for following Pinnacle\'s instructions in all circumstances --- including situations where the bank\'s own negligence contributed to the loss --- is not acceptable.
**[SECTION 6 --- BANK SET-OFF RIGHTS]{.underline}**
**[6.1 --- Pinnacle\'s Preferred Position (Green)]{.underline}**
Pinnacle\'s form ACA requires full subordination of the bank\'s liens and set-off rights in the controlled accounts to the Secured Party\'s security interest. The form language provides:

> *\"The Bank hereby subordinates all liens, security interests, encumbrances, claims, counterclaims, and rights of set-off that the Bank may now or hereafter have in or with respect to the Accounts and the funds on deposit therein to the security interest of the Secured Party.\"*

The rationale for this provision is straightforward: Pinnacle\'s security interest in the controlled accounts should be first-priority. If the bank can exercise set-off rights against controlled account balances --- for example, to satisfy unpaid loan obligations, treasury management fees, or other amounts owed by the Depositor to the bank --- Pinnacle\'s collateral can be diminished without notice to or consent of Pinnacle, potentially at the very moment when the borrower is in financial distress and the collateral is most needed to support Pinnacle\'s recovery. Full subordination eliminates this risk by ensuring that the bank\'s claims are junior to Pinnacle\'s security interest in all circumstances.

The priority rule of UCC § 9-327 reinforces Pinnacle\'s position: under § 9-327(1), a security interest held by a secured party that has control of a deposit account has priority over a conflicting security interest held by a secured party that does not have control. However, under § 9-327(3), a security interest held by the depository bank itself has priority over a security interest held by another secured party, even if the other secured party has control. This means that absent a contractual subordination, the bank\'s own security interest in the deposit account --- which arises by operation of the bank\'s relationship with the depositor --- would have priority over Pinnacle\'s security interest. The subordination provision in the ACA is designed to contractually override this statutory priority rule by requiring the bank to subordinate its claims. UCC § 9-339 permits such subordination by agreement.
**[6.2 --- Common Bank Pushback]{.underline}**

Banks virtually always resist full subordination of their set-off rights. The negotiation of the set-off provision is typically one of the most contentious aspects of ACA negotiation and often consumes a disproportionate share of the negotiation timeline. Common bank positions include:

> • **Preservation of Set-Off for All Depositor Obligations.** The bank seeks to preserve its right of set-off for \"any obligation owed to the Bank by the Depositor, whether direct or contingent, now existing or hereafter arising.\" This formulation is maximally broad and would permit the bank to set off against controlled account balances for obligations arising under credit facilities, loan agreements, letter of credit reimbursement obligations, treasury management agreements, and any other banking relationship between the bank and the Depositor --- including contingent or unliquidated obligations.

25: **WHEREAS**, Depositor maintains one or more deposit accounts at Bank, each as more particularly identified and described on Schedule A attached hereto and incorporated herein by reference (collectively, the \"Accounts\" and each individually, an \"Account\");

27: **WHEREAS**, Secured Party has been granted a security interest in, and lien upon, such Accounts and all funds, cash, instruments, investment property, and other property at any time credited thereto, pursuant to that certain Credit Agreement dated as of **\_\_**, 20\_\_, by and between Depositor and Secured Party, as the same may be amended, restated, supplemented, or otherwise modified from time to time, together with all related security agreements, pledge agreements, guaranties, and ancillary documents executed in connection therewith (collectively, the \"Loan Documents\");
28: 
29: **WHEREAS**, the Parties desire to enter into this Agreement to establish \"control\" (as such term is defined and used in Articles 8 and 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code as in effect in the State of New York) by the Secured Party over the Accounts in order to perfect the security interest of the Secured Party therein; and
30: 
31: **WHEREAS**, Bank is willing to enter into this Agreement on the terms and conditions set forth herein.

33: **NOW, THEREFORE**, in consideration of the mutual covenants, representations, and agreements contained herein, and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the Parties hereby agree as follows:
34: 
35: **[Section 1 --- Definitions]{.underline}**
36: 
37: As used in this Agreement, the following terms shall have the meanings set forth below. Capitalized terms used but not otherwise defined in this Agreement shall have the meanings ascribed to them in the Loan Documents or, if not defined therein, in the UCC.
38: 
39: **\"Account\"** or **\"Deposit Account\"** means each deposit account identified on Schedule A hereto, including any and all renewals, replacements, reclassifications, redesignations, or successor accounts thereof, howsoever denominated, and all funds, cash, instruments, chattel paper, investment property, general intangibles, and other property at any time credited to, deposited in, held in, or otherwise attributable to any such account, together with all interest, dividends, income, and other earnings thereon and all proceeds (as defined in the UCC) thereof.
40: 
41: **\"Business Day\"** means any day on which Bank is open for the conduct of substantially all of its commercial banking business at its offices in New York, New York, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and any day on which banking institutions in the State of New York are authorized or required by law or executive order to close.
42: 
43: **\"Entitlement Order\"** has the meaning ascribed to such term in UCC Section 8-102(a)(8), and shall include any notification communicated to Bank directing the transfer, redemption, liquidation, or other disposition of a financial asset or interest therein, including without limitation any instruction originated by Secured Party pursuant to Section 3 of this Agreement.
44: 
45: **\"Event of Default\"** means an \"Event of Default\" as defined in, and determined in accordance with, the Loan Documents, or as otherwise notified by Secured Party to Bank pursuant to a Notice of Exclusive Control delivered in accordance with the terms of this Agreement. For the avoidance of doubt, Bank shall have no obligation or duty to independently determine whether an Event of Default has occurred or is continuing under the Loan Documents.
46: 
47: **\"Exclusive Control Notice\"** or **\"Notice of Exclusive Control\"** (each, an **\"NOEC\"**) means a written notice delivered by Secured Party to Bank in accordance with Section 10 hereof, substantially in the form attached hereto as Exhibit A (if any), asserting that an Event of Default has occurred under the Loan Documents and directing Bank to comply exclusively with Instructions originated by or on behalf of Secured Party with respect to the Accounts, and to cease complying with any and all Instructions originated by or on behalf of Depositor.
48: 
49: **\"Instructions\"** means any order, direction, instruction, request, or authorization regarding the disposition of funds in, or any other action to be taken or omitted with respect to, any Account, including without limitation directions to initiate or execute wire transfers, ACH transactions, checks, withdrawals, transfers between accounts, account closings, and the provision of account statements, balance information, and other account-related information.
50: 
51: **\"Lien\"** means any security interest, lien, pledge, hypothecation, charge, mortgage, encumbrance, attachment, garnishment, levy, claim, right of set-off, right of recoupment, banker\'s lien, right of combination of accounts, or other interest or right of any kind, whether arising by contract, operation of law, equity, or otherwise.
52: 
53: **\"Loan Documents\"** means, collectively, the credit agreement, loan agreement, security agreement, and all related agreements, instruments, certificates, and documents between or among Depositor and Secured Party (and any guarantors or other obligors party thereto), as the same may be amended, restated, amended and restated, supplemented, replaced, refinanced, or otherwise modified from time to time, including without limitation any intercreditor agreements, subordination agreements, and collateral documents executed in connection therewith.
54: 
55: **\"UCC\"** means the Uniform Commercial Code as in effect from time to time in the State of New York; provided that, to the extent that the UCC is used to define any term herein and such term is defined differently in different Articles or Divisions of the UCC, the definition of such term contained in Article 9 shall govern. In the event that, by reason of mandatory provisions of law, any of the attachment, perfection, or priority of the Secured Party\'s security interest in any Account is governed by the Uniform Commercial Code as enacted and in effect in a jurisdiction other than the State of New York, the term \"UCC\" shall mean the Uniform Commercial Code as enacted and in effect in such other jurisdiction solely for purposes of the provisions hereof relating to such attachment, perfection, or priority and for purposes of definitions relating to such provisions.
56: 
57: All other capitalized terms used in this Agreement and not specifically defined herein shall have the meanings assigned to such terms in the Loan Documents. To the extent a term is defined both in this Agreement and in the Loan Documents, the definition set forth in this Agreement shall control for purposes of this Agreement.

59: **[Section 2 --- The Accounts; Establishment of Control]{.underline}**
60: 
61: **2.1 Confirmation of Accounts.** Bank hereby confirms and acknowledges that (a) each Account listed on Schedule A hereto is maintained at Bank, (b) each such Account is held in the name of Depositor as the account holder of record, (c) each such Account constitutes a \"deposit account\" and/or \"securities account\" (as applicable) within the meaning of the UCC, and (d) Bank is the \"bank\" (as defined in UCC Section 9-102(a)(8)) with respect to each such Account.
62: 
63: **2.2 Establishment of Control.** Bank hereby agrees that, from and after the Effective Date, it will comply with Instructions originated by Secured Party directing the disposition of funds in the Accounts without further consent of Depositor, thereby establishing \"control\" by Secured Party over the Accounts within the meaning of UCC Sections 9-104(a)(2) and 8-106 (to the extent applicable). Bank acknowledges and agrees that such compliance obligation is unconditional and shall not be subject to any conditions precedent other than the delivery of such Instructions in a manner consistent with Section 10 of this Agreement. 281: **11.4 Bank Resignation.** Bank may resign from its obligations under this Agreement upon thirty (30) days\' prior written notice to Secured Party and Depositor, delivered in accordance with Section 10 hereof; *provided*, however, that such resignation shall not be effective, and Bank shall continue to be bound by all of its obligations under this Agreement, until each of the following conditions has been satisfied: (a) a successor depository bank acceptable to Secured Party in its reasonable discretion has been identified and appointed, (b) all Accounts (and all funds therein) have been transferred to successor accounts at such successor depository bank, and (c) a replacement deposit account control agreement in form and substance satisfactory to Secured Party in its reasonable discretion has been duly executed and delivered by Depositor, Secured Party, and the successor depository bank. Bank shall cooperate fully with Secured Party and Depositor in connection with the transition to a successor depository bank, including without limitation by providing account statements, transaction histories, and such other information and documentation as Secured Party may reasonably request.
282: 
283: **11.5 Survival.** The provisions of Section 5 (Subordination of Bank Liens; Waiver of Set-Off), Section 7 (Secured Party Indemnification of Bank), Section 8 (Limitation of Liability), Section 12 (Governing Law; Jurisdiction; Miscellaneous), and this Section 11.5 shall survive the termination of this Agreement for any reason, to the extent applicable.
284: 
285: **[Section 12 --- Governing Law; Jurisdiction; Miscellaneous]{.underline}**
286: 
287: **Section 12.1 --- Governing Law**
288: 
289: This Agreement shall be governed by, and construed and interpreted in accordance with, the laws of the State of New York, without regard to any conflict-of-laws principles thereof that would require or permit the application of the laws of any other jurisdiction. To the extent not governed by the internal laws of the State of New York, matters relating to the perfection, priority, and enforcement of security interests in the Accounts shall be determined in accordance with the UCC as in effect in the applicable jurisdiction determined pursuant to UCC Section 9-304.
290: 
291: **Section 12.2 --- Jurisdiction; Venue**
292: 
293: Each Party hereto irrevocably and unconditionally submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and the Supreme Court of the State of New York, County of New York (Borough of Manhattan), and any appellate courts thereof, for the purpose of any action, suit, or proceeding arising out of or relating to this Agreement, and each Party hereby irrevocably and unconditionally waives, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, any objection that it may now or hereafter have to the laying of venue of any such action, suit, or proceeding in any such court, and any claim that any such action, suit, or proceeding has been brought in an inconvenient forum. Each Party consents to service of process in any manner permitted by applicable law.
294: 
295: **Section 12.3 --- Waiver of Jury Trial**
296: 
297: **EACH PARTY HERETO HEREBY IRREVOCABLY AND UNCONDITIONALLY WAIVES, TO THE FULLEST EXTENT PERMITTED BY APPLICABLE LAW, ANY AND ALL RIGHT TO TRIAL BY JURY IN ANY ACTION, SUIT, PROCEEDING, CLAIM, OR COUNTERCLAIM ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT OR THE TRANSACTIONS CONTEMPLATED HEREBY, WHETHER BASED ON CONTRACT, TORT, OR ANY OTHER THEORY. EACH PARTY ACKNOWLEDGES THAT THIS WAIVER IS A MATERIAL INDUCEMENT TO THE OTHER PARTIES\' ENTERING INTO THIS AGREEMENT, THAT EACH PARTY HAS BEEN AFFORDED THE OPPORTUNITY TO CONSULT WITH LEGAL COUNSEL REGARDING THIS WAIVER, AND THAT THIS WAIVER SHALL BE EFFECTIVE TO THE FULLEST EXTENT PERMITTED BY LAW.**
298: 
299: **Section 12.4 --- Amendments**
300: 
301: No amendment, modification, supplement, restatement, or waiver of any provision of this Agreement shall be effective unless set forth in a written instrument duly executed and delivered by each of the three Parties hereto. No waiver of any provision of this Agreement shall constitute a waiver of any other provision (whether or not similar), nor shall any such waiver constitute a continuing waiver unless otherwise expressly provided in writing.
302: 
303: **Section 12.5 --- Entire Agreement**
304: 
305: This Agreement, together with the Schedules and Exhibits attached hereto and incorporated herein by reference, constitutes the entire agreement among the Parties with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements, representations, warranties, understandings, negotiations, and discussions, whether written or oral, among the Parties with respect to such subject matter. There are no conditions, warranties, representations, or other agreements among the Parties in connection with the subject matter of this Agreement, whether oral or written, express or implied, except as specifically set forth herein.
306: 
307: **Section 12.6 --- Severability**
308: 
309: If any provision of this Agreement is held to be invalid, illegal, or unenforceable in any respect under any applicable law, rule, or regulation in any jurisdiction, such invalidity, illegality, or unenforceability shall not affect the validity, legality, or enforceability of any other provision of this Agreement or the validity, legality, or enforceability of such provision in any other jurisdiction. In the event of any such determination, the Parties shall negotiate in good faith to modify this Agreement so as to effect the original intent of the Parties as closely as possible in an acceptable manner, so that the transactions contemplated hereby are consummated as originally contemplated to the greatest extent possible.
310: 
311: **Section 12.7 --- Counterparts; Electronic Execution**
312: 
313: This Agreement may be executed in any number of counterparts, each of which shall be deemed to be an original, and all of which, when taken together, shall constitute one and the same instrument. Delivery of an executed counterpart of a signature page to this Agreement by facsimile transmission, by electronic mail in \"portable document format\" (.pdf) form, or by any other electronic means intended to preserve the original graphic and pictorial appearance of a document, shall be effective as delivery of an originally executed counterpart of this Agreement. The words \"execution,\" \"signed,\" \"signature,\" and words of similar import in or relating to this Agreement shall be deemed to include electronic signatures, deliveries, or the keeping of records in electronic form, each of which shall be of the same legal effect, validity, or enforceability as a manually executed signature, physical delivery thereof, or the use of a paper-based recordkeeping system, to the extent and as provided for in any applicable law, including the Federal Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act, the New York State Electronic Signatures and Records Act, and any other similar state laws based on the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act.
314: 
315: **Section 12.8 --- Successors and Assigns**
316: 
317: This Agreement shall be binding upon, and shall inure to the benefit of, the Parties hereto and their respective successors, legal representatives, and permitted assigns. Depositor may not assign, delegate, or transfer any of its rights, interests, or obligations under this Agreement without the prior written consent of Secured Party. Secured Party may freely assign, delegate, or transfer any or all of its rights, interests, and obligations under this Agreement, in whole or in part, to any successor, assignee, transferee, or participant under the Loan Documents or otherwise, without the consent of Depositor or Bank, and any such assignee or transferee shall thereupon be vested with all the rights, powers, and remedies of Secured Party hereunder as if originally named as Secured Party herein. Secured Party shall notify Bank in writing of any such assignment or transfer within a commercially reasonable time following the effectiveness thereof.
